one_liner: crypto-js API with the hash and cipher block functions ported to Rust/WebAssembly; big wins only for SHA-512/384 and SHA-3.
what_it_does: A re-implementation of crypto-js (same CryptoJSW.MD5(...), SHA256(...), AES.encrypt(msg, passphrase) calls, WordArray, enc, mode, pad and format objects) whose per-block work runs in WebAssembly, for browsers and Node.js. Each algorithm must be initialised once with the async X.loadWasm() (or loadAllWasm()) before the otherwise synchronous calls work. It covers MD5, SHA-1/224/256/384/512, crypto-js's SHA3 (Keccak), RIPEMD-160, HMAC, PBKDF2, EvpKDF, AES, DES, TripleDES, Blowfish, Rabbit, RC4, plus an RSA API (OAEP/PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption, PSS/PKCS#1 v1.5 signatures) that crypto-js lacks.
how_it_is_fast: Each algorithm's block loop is a line-by-line Rust port of the crypto-js code, built with wasm-pack (release profile opt-level 3, LTO) and shipped as pako-deflated base64 inside the JS bundle. The JS wrapper keeps crypto-js's buffering, padding and string/WordArray handling, copies the buffered words into wasm linear memory through wasm-bindgen glue and processes every ready block in one call. The large gains come where crypto-js emulates 64-bit arithmetic with X64Word objects: the Rust SHA-512/384 uses native u64, and SHA-3 keeps its 25 lanes as high/low u32 pairs in a stack array rather than heap objects. AES, DES and Blowfish are the same table-driven scalar algorithms as crypto-js; there is no SIMD.
when_to_use: An existing crypto-js code base that must keep byte-identical outputs (WordArray API, OpenSSL-format passphrase AES, crypto-js's Keccak 'SHA3') and spends its time in SHA-512, SHA-384 or SHA3 over inputs of a megabyte or more: about 4-5x (SHA-512/384) and 4-17x (SHA3) in the published charts.
TripleDES, DES, MD5 or RIPEMD-160 over large strings in legacy crypto-js code, where the charts show roughly 1.3-2x.
Browser or Node.js code that can await one asynchronous initialisation at startup and then needs synchronous crypto-js-style calls (WebCrypto's SubtleCrypto is async-only).
Needing crypto-js-style RSA (key generation, OAEP, PSS) in the same API, local use only (see gotchas).
when_not_to_use: AES: slower than crypto-js in all three published charts (Chrome, Firefox, Node); SHA-1, SHA-224/256, Rabbit and RC4 gain only about 1.05-1.15x; the maintainer confirmed in issue #11 that DES decryption was slower than crypto-js in Chrome 116 and blamed the JS-to-wasm copy overhead.

New code without a crypto-js compatibility constraint: WebCrypto (native AES-GCM, SHA-2, PBKDF2) or a dedicated wasm hash library is much faster; the sibling hash-wasm reports 426 MB/s for SHA-256 on 1 MB inputs, while this library's charts are within 10% of crypto-js there.
Anything that needs FIPS 202 SHA-3, modern AEAD modes, or the CTRGladman mode with AES/DES/Blowfish (see gotchas); many covered algorithms (MD5, SHA-1, DES, RC4, Rabbit) are legacy and insecure.
Server-side RSA decryption reachable by attackers: it uses the Rust rsa crate 0.6.1, affected by RUSTSEC-2023-0071 (Marvin timing attack, no patched version).
Projects needing active maintenance: last commit 2024-06-25 (v1.1.1), seven open issues, and an open report that tree-shaking does not work (issue #17).

integration.form: module (npm package @originjs/crypto-js-wasm, ESM source built as UMD, wasm binaries inlined as base64)
integration.dependencies: pako at runtime (inflates the embedded wasm); package.json also lists 'add' and 'global' as dependencies; rebuilding the wasm needs a Rust toolchain plus wasm-pack
integration.min_toolchain: Any JS runtime with WebAssembly.instantiate; minimum browser and Node versions not documented (charts used Chrome 102, Firefox 101, Node labelled v16.6.4); rustc and wasm-pack versions not stated
integration.platforms: Browsers and Node.js with WebAssembly (README); Cloudflare Workers support was requested in issue #22 (closed 2026-02-03)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each algorithm keeps one module-wide wasm instance in a static field, so use one instance per JS thread/worker
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same API and outputs as crypto-js for the tested paths, but every algorithm needs an awaited loadWasm()/loadAllWasm() first (otherwise 'WASM is not loaded yet' is thrown), and v1.1.1 changed the PBKDF2 defaults to SHA-256 with 250,000 iterations (crypto-js 4.2.0 behaviour, not 4.1.1), while the README still says SHA-1

gotchas: Silent no-encryption bug (code reading of rust/aes/src/lib.rs, not executed): the Rust doEncrypt/doDecrypt dispatch on mode._name.to_lowercase() and handle only cbc, ecb, cfb, ofb and ctr; any other mode, including the exported CTRGladman, falls into '_ => {}' and leaves the data words unchanged, so AES.encrypt(..., { mode: CTRGladman }) returns the padded plaintext as 'ciphertext'. The DES and Blowfish crates have the same fall-through. A round-trip test (like the benchmark's own equality check) would not catch it.

Block counting in float32 (rust/md5, sha1, sha256, sha3 doCrypt: 'dataSigBytes as f32 / blockSizeBytes as f32'): above 16 MiB of buffered data the count can be off by one. Emulating the Rust f32 arithmetic: a streaming update() with 16,777,279 buffered bytes counts 262,145 SHA-256 blocks instead of 262,144 (a partial block is compressed as full, wrong digest), at 134,217,785 bytes it indexes past the slice (wasm trap), and a one-shot SHA3-512 of 134,217,864 bytes drops the final padded block. One-shot MD5/SHA-1/SHA-256 stay exact below about 1 GiB; the 1 MiB benchmark is unaffected.

Compatibility quirks inherited from crypto-js: 'SHA3' pads with 0x01 (original Keccak), so it does not match FIPS 202 SHA3-512; CTR mode increments only the last 32-bit counter word; AES uses lookup tables (SubMix/SBOX), so it is not constant-time. RSA defaults to a 1024-bit key when generating (docs/rsa.md).

Every _process call copies the whole buffered JS word array into wasm linear memory and copies state back; wasm memory grows to the largest message and never shrinks. String-to-WordArray conversion, padding and splicing stay in JS, which is why the cheap algorithms barely move (Node chart, derived from page data: wasm MD5 ~270 ms and SHA-256 ~330 ms per loop against ~118 ms for wasm SHA3-512, so glue, not the Rust kernel, dominates).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over hash-wasm only when you must keep crypto-js's API and outputs (WordArray, OpenSSL-format passphrase AES, crypto-js's Keccak 'SHA3', HMAC/PBKDF2/EvpKDF wiring); for plain hashing hash-wasm is several times faster and has a streaming TypedArray API, and fast-noble-hashes or awasm-noble are the faster route for @noble/hashes users.
verified_claims_summary: First-party bar charts (README; i5-4590, Windows 10 21H2): average time per timed loop of identical crypto-js-style calls on 1 MiB random alphanumeric strings (the public Node harness uses one string, 1 warm-up and 10 timed loops; which harness version and package version produced the 2022 charts is not stated). crypto-js-wasm versus crypto-js: SHA3 ~103 vs ~1775 ms in Chrome 102 (~17x, a Chrome-specific crypto-js slowdown; ~4x in Firefox 101 and ~5.7x in Node), SHA-512 ~4-5x, MD5 ~1.5-2x, SHA-1/SHA-256/Rabbit/RC4 ~1.05-1.15x, AES slower everywhere; RSA about 2x faster than jsencrypt in Chrome.
status_note: Stale since 2024-06-25 (v1.1.1) with seven open issues; Mulan PSL v2 (OSI-approved permissive), usable as a crypto-js speed-up for 64-bit hashes, but the AES mode fall-through and float32 block counting found in the source are unfixed.
